```{r}
#Dataset and main library
tunnel_data<-read.csv("statcast_bat_tracking_2024_2025.csv")
library(tidyverse)
#Quadratic Formula function
quad<- function(a, b, c) {
  discriminant <- b^2 - 4 * a * c
  root <- (-b - sqrt(discriminant)) / (2 * a)
  return(root)
}
```

## Introduction and Prior Work:

When I did my investigation into fastball characteristics and whiff
rates one major factor outside of our analysis was how a pitchers
fastball interacts with their other pitches. Pitches do not exist in a
vacuum. The success of a pitch can be heavily dependent on the profile
of the previous pitch. For example Greg Maddux’s individual pitches
weren’t overwhelming. But he threw them in a way that they looked the
same for as long as possible on their path to the plate, before breaking
apart at the last second. This approach, which was wildly successful for
Maddux, is known as pitch tunneling. 

Tunneling is very well known in the baseball world, but there are
surprisingly few accessible metrics that capture it. There is no Stuff+
or Location+ equivalent for tunneling. 

The main metric I could find that attempted to quantify tunneling was
from Baseball Prospectus in 2017 and was a big inspiration for my
project. They created something called “Tunnel Differential”, which is
the distance between two pitches at the point where the hitter has to
make a swing decision. They called this point the “Tunnel Point” and
measured it to be about 175 milliseconds before contact which translates
to about 23.8 feet before the plate (the tunnel point I used for my own
calculations). They also measured the difference at release between
several pitches and how much a pitch moves after the tunnel point. 

Another more recent metric that I found is Driveline’s Match+. Match+
essentially evaluates the overall similarity of a pitchers arsenal out
of the hand, using continuous 3D trajectory modeling. 

Both of these metrics have immense merit, but they left a gap I wanted
to explore. My goal was to create an all-in one metric to evaluate the
full flight of individual pitches instead of arsenals. This would then
allow me not only see and create overlays of some of the nastiest
tunnels but also determine what pitchers actively tunnel the best on an
individual pitch basis rather than just have the best tunneling stuff.

## Data and Data Manipulation:

Statcast data from Baseball Savant offers incredibly precise pitch
tracking data. I was able to download a dataset of all pitches from the
2024 and 2025 MLB season from a user on Kaggle which gave me everything
I needed to conduct the analysis. Rather than the computationally
expensive and complicated continuous pitch tracking used by Driveline I
used a similar approach to Baseball Prospectus. Using kinematics and the
release point, end point, velocity, and acceleration data given by
Stacast, I calculated each pitch's position at four discrete points
along its trajectory:

1.  Release

2.  Early Flight (40 feet from the plate)

3.  The Tunnel Point (28.3 feet from the plate)

4.  Home Plate

Using these calculated positions I then grouped each pitch by at bat,
and then calculated the difference between each pitch and the previous
pitch’s position at all four checkpoints.

```{r}
#Adding in_zone variable (Used later for Regression)
tunnel_data<-tunnel_data%>%
  mutate(
    in_zone_x = ifelse(abs(plate_x) <= 0.708, 1, 0),
    in_zone_z = ifelse(plate_z >= sz_bot & plate_z <= sz_top, 1, 0),
    in_zone = ifelse(in_zone_x == 1 & in_zone_z == 1, 1, 0)
  )
```

```{r}
#Finding Position at the Tunnel Point
tunnel_data<-tunnel_data %>%
  mutate(
    y0=60.5-release_extension,
    d=y0-23.8,
    t_tunnel= quad(0.5*ay,vy0,d),
    tunnel_x = release_pos_x + (vx0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * ax * (t_tunnel^2)),
    tunnel_z = release_pos_z + (vz0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * az * (t_tunnel^2))
  )
```

```{r}
#Finding Position Early in Trajectory (40 feet) 
tunnel_data<-tunnel_data %>%
  mutate(
    y0=60.5-release_extension,
    d40=y0-40,
    t40= quad(0.5*ay,vy0,d40),
    x40 = release_pos_x + (vx0 * t40) + (0.5 * ax * (t40^2)),
    z40 = release_pos_z + (vz0 * t40) + (0.5 * az * (t40^2))
  )
```

```{r}
#Grouping Consecutive Pitches Together and finding differences
paired_pitches <- tunnel_data %>%
  arrange(player_name, game_pk, at_bat_number, pitch_number) %>%
  group_by(game_pk, at_bat_number) %>%
  mutate(
    prev_pitch_type = lag(pitch_type),
    prev_pitch_velo = lag(release_speed),
    prev_release_x = lag(release_pos_x),
    prev_release_z = lag(release_pos_z),
    prev_x40 = lag(x40),
    prev_z40 = lag (z40),
    prev_tunnel_x = lag(tunnel_x),
    prev_tunnel_z = lag(tunnel_z),
    prev_plate_x = lag(plate_x),
    prev_plate_z = lag(plate_z),
    prev_pfx_x = lag(pfx_x),
    prev_pfx_z = lag(pfx_z),
    prev_pitch_in_zone=lag(in_zone),
    release_diff = sqrt((release_pos_x - prev_release_x)^2 + (release_pos_z - prev_release_z)^2),
    early_diff = sqrt((x40 - prev_x40)^2 + (z40 - prev_z40)^2),
    tunnel_diff = sqrt((tunnel_x - prev_tunnel_x)^2 + (tunnel_z - prev_tunnel_z)^2),
    plate_diff = sqrt((plate_x - prev_plate_x)^2 + (plate_z - prev_plate_z)^2),
    velo_diff = release_speed-prev_pitch_velo,
    movement_diff=sqrt((pfx_x-prev_pfx_x)^2+(pfx_z-prev_pfx_z)^2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  drop_na(release_diff, early_diff, tunnel_diff, plate_diff, velo_diff, movement_diff)%>%
  filter(pitch_type!=prev_pitch_type)
```

## Dimension Reduction:

Naturally, these four variables have high covariance. A pitch's position
at release is extremely correlated with its position at 40 feet, and so
on. To account for this I ran a Principal Component Analysis on the four
variables which was something I saw in one of the papers we looked at
for my Applied Statistical Modeling class and wanted to try out. It
worked exceptionally well. The first two components not only represented
88.05% of the variation, but they perfectly matched real-world pitch
qualities:

- PC1 (Overall Separation): Had entirely positive loadings, with the
  heaviest weight placed on the distance between pitches at the tunnel
  point. This component represents the overall separation between the
  two pitches.

- PC2 (The Late Break): The loadings for the distance between the
  pitches at release and at 40 feet were positive, while the loadings
  for the distance at the tunnel point and at the plate were negative
  (with the distance at the plate being twice as heavily weighted). This
  component can be interpreted as the late break of the pitch.

#### PCA Output

```{r}
#Running the PCA
pca_model <- prcomp(~ release_diff + early_diff + tunnel_diff+ plate_diff, 
  data = paired_pitches, 
  center = TRUE,
  scale. = TRUE,
)
#|echo: true
#Variance
summary(pca_model)

#Loadings
pca_model$rotation
```

```{r}
#Clean Data and Apply PCA
tunnel_plus_data<-paired_pitches %>%
  drop_na(effective_speed, pfx_x, pfx_z, plate_x, plate_z, delta_pitcher_run_exp, movement_diff)%>%
  filter(pitch_type != "", !is.na(pitch_type))%>%
  bind_cols(as_tibble(predict(pca_model, newdata = .))) %>%
  rename(
    Overall_Separation_PC1 = PC1,
    Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2 = PC2)%>%
  mutate(
    PC1_z = as.numeric(scale(Overall_Separation_PC1)),
    PC2_z = as.numeric(scale(Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2)),
    score=(PC1_z+PC2_z)*-1,
    Standardized_Score=scale(score),
    is_whiff=ifelse(description %in% c("swinging_strike", "swinging_strike_blocked", "missed_bunt"), 1, 0),
    is_called_strike=ifelse(description == "called_strike", 1, 0),
  )
#Find baselines for calculating Tunnel+ for 2026 data and my own data
PC1mean<-mean(tunnel_plus_data$Overall_Separation_PC1)
PC1sd<-sd(tunnel_plus_data$Overall_Separation_PC1)
PC2mean<-mean(tunnel_plus_data$Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2)
PC2sd<-sd(tunnel_plus_data$Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2)
combinedmean<-mean(tunnel_plus_data$score)
combinedsd<-sd(tunnel_plus_data$score)
```

```{r}
#Inital Regression Model
regression_model<-lm(delta_pitcher_run_exp ~ Overall_Separation_PC1+Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2, data = tunnel_plus_data)
```

```{r}
#Models Illustratiing effectiveness
tunnel_model <- lm(delta_pitcher_run_exp ~ Standardized_Score, data = tunnel_plus_data)
contact_model<-lm(estimated_woba_using_speedangle~Standardized_Score, data = tunnel_plus_data)
whiff_model<-glm(is_whiff~Standardized_Score, data=tunnel_plus_data, family=binomial)
called_strike_model<-glm(is_called_strike~Standardized_Score, data=tunnel_plus_data, family=binomial)
```

```{r}
#Best Tunnels
best_tunnels<-tunnel_plus_data%>%
  #Shows what initial regression thinks of the tunnel
  mutate(
     regression_score=predict(regression_model)
  )%>%
  select(
    player_name,      
    batter,         
    game_date,    
    game_pk,          
    at_bat_number,    
    pitch_number,     
    inning,           
    balls,
    strikes,
    pitch_type,
    release_speed,
    prev_pitch_type,
    prev_pitch_velo,
    Standardized_Score,
    release_diff,
    early_diff,
    tunnel_diff,
    plate_diff,
    velo_diff,
    pfx_x,
    pfx_z,
    prev_pfx_x,
    prev_pfx_z,
    Overall_Separation_PC1,
    Late_Break_Tunnel_PC2,
    movement_diff,
    delta_pitcher_run_exp,
    regression_score
  )%>%
  arrange((desc(Standardized_Score)))
```

## Creating Tunnel+:

Using these two components I then ran a linear regression model
predicting delta_pitcher_run_exp (Statcast’s metric that represents the
change in run expectancy based on a particular pitch). This is similar
to how metrics like Stuff+ and Command+ from FanGraphs are created.
Unfortunately the “Tunneling” the model liked didn’t match the
conventional definition of tunneling. The coefficient for PC1 was
positive and significant indicating that the model preferred pitches
with low separation, however the coefficient for PC2 was positive, and
since the loadings for the distance between the pitches at the tunnel
point and at the plate were negative this meant that the model preferred
pitches with low late break. 

Tunneling is best illustrated through pitch overlays and because
Baseball Savant has video clips for each pitch I built a relatively
simple video overlayer in Python using the Movie.py library. Here is a
clip of the best tunneled pitch as seen by this model:

#### Freddy Peralta Changeup and Fourseam

<script>
document.write(`
  <video controls autoplay loop muted playsinline width="100%">
    <source src="https://jsadowskivassar.github.io/Tunnel-Plus/PeraltaOverlay.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  </video>
`);
</script>

These pitches are essentially the opposite of tunneled. They come from
completely different release points 9 inches apart, and then cross paths
around the Tunnel Point and end up within 2 inches at the Plate. The two
pitches start far apart and then end up close together instead of
starting close together and ending far apart.

I believe one reason the regression model opted for pitches with low
plate distances is because pitches that end up far apart are much more
likely to be balls and unappealing to swing at. To counteract this I
tried adding an interaction term between PC2 and the pitch being in the
strike zone. Sure enough the coefficient for PC2 was negative when the
pitch was in the zone indicating that in this case more late break is
better. This was a better result but still not entirely what I wanted as
a good tunnel doesn’t necessarily have to end in the strike zone.

My next strategy was aggregating the z-scores of PC1 and PC2. Equally
weighting and adding the overall separation and late break ensures that
what is thought of as a traditional tunnel, two pitches that look
exactly the same for the beginning of their flight before aggressively
breaking away from each other, was rewarded. This strategy was much more
successful and generated some really good overlays:

#### Zach Wheeler Sinker and Fourseam

<script>
document.write(`
  <video controls autoplay loop muted playsinline width="100%">
    <source src="https://jsadowskivassar.github.io/Tunnel-Plus/WheelerOverlay.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  </video>
`);
</script>

This was the highest scored tunnel in the dataset. Wheeler's 97mph
fourseam and 96mph sinker come from the exact same release point, are
0.18 inches apart at 40 feet and 2 inches apart at the tunnel point.
After the tunnel point the fourseam stays on plane while the sinker
drops ending up 8.5 inches below the fourseam. It's hard to see in the
video but the batter Martin Maldonato takes the first sinker for a
strike and then likely identifies the following fourseam as the same
exact pitch causing him to swing under it, illustrating the
effectiveness of tunneling.

#### Brock Stewart Fourseam and Cutter

<script>
document.write(`
  <video controls autoplay loop muted playsinline width="100%">
    <source src="https://jsadowskivassar.github.io/Tunnel-Plus/BrockStewartOverlay.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  </video>
`);
</script>

The first pitch in this sequence was a dotted 96mph fastball that should
have been called a strike but unfortunately was a ball. The next pitch,
a 92mph cutter, once again comes from the exact same release point and
is within 0.3 inches at 40 feet and 2 inches at the tunnel point before
cutting in and ending up lower and closer to the middle of the plate.
This difference combined with a 4mph velocity difference results in
another swing and miss.

#### Adrian Houser Sinker and Slider

<script>
document.write(`
  <video controls autoplay loop muted playsinline width="100%">
    <source src="https://jsadowskivassar.github.io/Tunnel-Plus/HouserOverlay.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  </video>
`);

My favorite overlay from the highest rated tunnels is Adrian Houser's
90mph sinker and 82mph slider. These pitches come from the same release
point, are within 0.1 inches at 40 feet, and are still within 4 inches
at the tunnel point. Then the sinker darts inside to the righty batter
while the slider sweeps outside ending 17 inches apart. Even though
batter Jared Triolo impressively manages to lay off the low and away
slider, this sequence makes for an incredible overlay.

## Does Tunneling Matter:

In addition to passing the eye test this tunneling metric was also shown
to impact the game itself. Good tunneling was associated with a higher
probability of a swing and miss or called strike, lower quality contact,
and run prevention. 

For individual pitches, a one standard deviation increase in Tunnel
Score (10 point increase in Tunnel+) was associated with:

- A 10.8% increase in swing and miss probability 

- A 3.7% increase in called strike probability

- A 0.005 point decrease in Expected wOBA on contact (xwOBAcon)

- Preventing 0.006 more runs

While 0.005 points of xwOBAcon and 0.006 runs may seem small, it is
important to remember that these values apply to each individual pitch.
Over the course of a full season where a starting pitcher throws around
2,500 pitches, a 0.005 point drop in xwOBAcon is highly significant.
Furthermore, preventing 0.006 runs per pitch equates to preventing an
extra 15 runs over a season. Since roughly 9 to 10 runs equals 1 Win
Above Replacement (WAR), a 1-standard-deviation increase in Tunnel+ is
worth roughly 1.5 to 1.6 WAR.

#### Impact of Tunnel+ on Pitch Outcomes

```{r}
#Table showing regression results of Tunnel+
library(modelsummary)
models <- list(
  "Whiff Prob (Logit)" = whiff_model,
  "Called Strike Prob (Logit)" = called_strike_model,
  "xwOBAcon (OLS)" = contact_model,
  "Run Expectancy (OLS)" = tunnel_model
)
modelsummary(
  models,
  stars = TRUE,
  statistic = NULL,
  coef_rename = c(
    "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
    "Standardized_Score" = "Tunnel Score (Std. Dev.)"
  ),
  gof_omit = 'DF|Deviance|AIC|BIC|Log.Lik.|RMSE|Num.Obs|R2|R2 Adj.' 
)

```

I also applied this same tunnel metric to pitches from the first week of
the 2026 MLB season. Good tunneling was once again associated with a
higher probability of a swing and miss or a called strike, lower
expected wOBA on contact, and run prevention. Even though the much
smaller sample size resulted in the run prevention coefficient being
only marginally significant (p=0.0894) and the xwOBAcon coefficient not
reaching statistical significance, the directional stability of the
coefficients is highly encouraging. It demonstrates that across multiple
years, tunneling is a meaningfully positive attribute for a pitcher.

## MLB Leaderboards:

### Pitch Sequences

One of my main goals for this project was determining what pitchers are
best at tunneling. To do so I grouped the data by pitcher and pitch
sequence and then calculated each sequence's median Tunnel score
(because tunnel scores are heavily skewed). The best pitch pairs are
littered with some of the best pitchers in the league and guys that
traditionally are considered good tunnelers including Zach Wheeler,
Kevin Gausman, and Aaron Nola. Wheeler’s sinker and splitter leads the
league with a Tunnel+ of 116. Here is the full leaderboard:

```{r}
#Shows best Tunneling pitches and some other metrics about these pitches
pitch_pair_leaderboard<-tunnel_plus_data %>%
  mutate(
    pitch_sequence = paste(prev_pitch_type, pitch_type, sep = " + ")
  ) %>%
  group_by(player_name, pitch_sequence) %>%
  filter(n() >= 50) %>% 
  summarize(
    total_thrown = n(),
    elite_tunnel_percent= sum(Standardized_Score>=0.50)/total_thrown,
    average_tunnel_value = median(score),
    tunnel_90 = quantile(score, probs = 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_woba= mean(estimated_woba_using_speedangle, na.rm=TRUE),
    whiff_percentage=mean(is_whiff),
    called_strike_percentage=mean(is_called_strike),
    run_value = mean(delta_pitcher_run_exp),
    movement_diff = mean(movement_diff),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Tunnel_Plus = round(100 + (scale(average_tunnel_value)[,1] * 10))) %>%
  arrange(desc(average_tunnel_value))
pairmean<-mean(pitch_pair_leaderboard$average_tunnel_value)
pairsd<-sd(pitch_pair_leaderboard$average_tunnel_value)

```

#### Pitch Sequence Tunnel+ Leaderboard

```{r}
#|echo: true
#Makes Interactive Leaderboard
library(DT)
datatable(pitch_pair_leaderboard%>%select(player_name, pitch_sequence, Tunnel_Plus), extensions = 'Scroller', options = list(scrollX = TRUE, scrollY = "400px",dom = 'ft', scroller=TRUE, deferRender = TRUE))
```

```{r}
#Regressions for Pitch Pairs (No Significant findings)
pair_contact_model<-lm(average_woba~average_tunnel_value, data = pitch_pair_leaderboard)
pair_whiff_model<-glm(whiff_percentage~average_tunnel_value, data=pitch_pair_leaderboard)
pair_called_strike_model<-lm(called_strike_percentage~average_tunnel_value, data=pitch_pair_leaderboard)
pair_run_value<-lm(run_value~average_tunnel_value, data=pitch_pair_leaderboard)
```

### Pitcher Arsenals

Next I scored each pitcher's overall arsenal by calculating a weighted
average of each of their sequences and usage. Here are some of the
standouts:

#### Tyler Rogers

Tyler Rogers had the highest Tunnel+ of 113. With a fastball averaging
83.2 mph (in the 1st percentile) Rogers relies primarily on deception to
get hitters out. As a result it is unsurprising that he grades out very
well in tunneling. What he lacks in velocity, especially for a reliever,
he makes up for due to his unusual submarine armslot, unusual pitch
shapes, and elite tunneling. Although it is worth noting that Rogers
only throws two pitches giving him the advantage of every pitch in his
small arsenal tunneling extremely well.

#### Bailey Ober

The second best Tunneler and the best tunneling starting pitcher with a
Tunnel+ of 112 was Bailey Ober. Initially I was a little surprised, but
after looking at Ober’s profile it definitely makes sense. Ober is
another pitcher that was able to be very effective despite low fastball
velocity. In 2024 he posted 91st percentile pitching run value, with a
fastball that averaged 91.7mph (16th percentile) and the next year would
decline to 90.3mph (6th percentile). Lacking velocity, Ober relied on
elite offspeeds and tunneling. His slider and fastball had a Tunnel+ of
113 and changeup and fastball had a Tunnel+ of 110.

#### Degrom and Alcantara

The two big names in the top 10 are Jacob Degrom and Sandy Alcantara.
These two pitchers are pretty much the opposite of Rogers and Ober. They
are both power pitchers who pair elite velocity and elite tunneling to
put up Cy Young winning numbers. Alcantara’s 98mph sinker and 92mph
changeup are almost identical until the hitter's decision point. Then
the changeup drops off the table while the sinker keeps riding up and
armside. This allowed Alcantara to generate extremely high weak contact
rates early in counts which resulted in his historic volume. In addition
to Alcantara’s sinker and changeup combo which has a Tunnel+ of 114, his
sinker also pairs exceptionally well with his slider with a Tunnel+ of
112. This fastball slider combo is Jacob Degrom’s bread and butter. His
99mph fastball with elite carry and 92mph slider with sharp late break
pair perfectly and had a Tunnel+ of 113. Even post elbow surgery where
Degrom’s stuff hasn’t fully reached 2021 levels his elite command and
tunneling allow him to remain one of the best pitchers in the league. 

#### Max Fried (The Anti-Tunneler)

As far as the worst tunnelers in the league, one in particular stood
out: perennial Cy Young candidate Max Fried. His well below league
average Tunnel+ of 85 is not something you would expect for a pitcher of
his caliber. This just goes to show that there are multiple ways to be
an effective pitcher. Max Fried’s arsenal relies on having a lot of high
quality pitches. He throws a fourseam, cutter, sinker, two-seam,
curveball, sweeper, and change-up all more than 10% of the time. His
fastballs tunnel decently well with his fourseam and sinker having a
Tunnel+ of 103. However none of his offspeeds tunnel very well. This is
exacerbated by Fried’s most used offspeed pitch being his relatively
loopy curveball which is a pitch that is more difficult to tunnel due to
it tending to pop-up out of the hand. Many pitchers that are known for
their curveballs are below league average at tunneling, for example
Clayton Kershaw had a Tunnel+ of 94 even with the data being from later
in his career where he had to rely more on tunneling. Despite not being
an elite tunneler Fried is still an elite pitcher due to having a deadly
arsenal of high stuff pitches.

```{r}
#Shows bes tunneling arsenals and some other metrics about these arsenals
arsenal_tunnel_leaderboard <- pitch_pair_leaderboard %>%
  group_by(player_name) %>%
  summarize(
    total_arsenal_pitches = sum(total_thrown),
    arsenal_tunnel_score = weighted.mean(average_tunnel_value, w = total_thrown),
    arsenal_tunnel_percent=weighted.mean(elite_tunnel_percent, w = total_thrown),
    arsenal_90=weighted.mean(tunnel_90, w = total_thrown),
    arsenal_woba=mean(average_woba),
    arsenal_whiff_rate=mean(whiff_percentage),
    arsenal_called_strike_rate=mean(called_strike_percentage),
    run_value = mean(run_value),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Tunnel_Plus = round(100 + (scale(arsenal_tunnel_score)[,1] * 10))) %>%
  filter(total_arsenal_pitches>=500)%>%
  arrange(desc(arsenal_tunnel_score))

```

#### Pitcher Arsenal Tunnel+ Leaderboard

```{r}
#Same process as with 2024/2025 data but with 2026 data
statcast_2026<-read.csv("savant_data.csv")
statcast_2026<-statcast_2026 %>%
  mutate(
    y0=60.5-release_extension,
    d=y0-23.8,
    t_tunnel= quad(0.5*ay,vy0,d),
    tunnel_x = release_pos_x + (vx0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * ax * (t_tunnel^2)),
    tunnel_z = release_pos_z + (vz0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * az * (t_tunnel^2)),
    d40=y0-40,
    t40= quad(0.5*ay,vy0,d40),
    x40 = release_pos_x + (vx0 * t40) + (0.5 * ax * (t40^2)),
    z40 = release_pos_z + (vz0 * t40) + (0.5 * az * (t40^2)),
    is_whiff=ifelse(description %in% c("swinging_strike", "swinging_strike_blocked", "missed_bunt"), 1, 0),
    is_called_strike=ifelse(description == "called_strike", 1, 0)
  )
paired_pitches_2026 <- statcast_2026 %>%
  arrange(player_name, game_pk, at_bat_number, pitch_number) %>%
  group_by(game_pk, at_bat_number) %>%
  mutate(
    prev_pitch_type = lag(pitch_type),
    prev_pitch_velo = lag(release_speed),
    prev_release_x = lag(release_pos_x),
    prev_release_z = lag(release_pos_z),
    prev_x40 = lag(x40),
    prev_z40 = lag (z40),
    prev_tunnel_x = lag(tunnel_x),
    prev_tunnel_z = lag(tunnel_z),
    prev_plate_x = lag(plate_x),
    prev_plate_z = lag(plate_z),
    prev_pfx_x = lag(pfx_x),
    prev_pfx_z = lag(pfx_z),
    release_diff = sqrt((release_pos_x - prev_release_x)^2 + (release_pos_z - prev_release_z)^2),
    early_diff = sqrt((x40 - prev_x40)^2 + (z40 - prev_z40)^2),
    tunnel_diff = sqrt((tunnel_x - prev_tunnel_x)^2 + (tunnel_z - prev_tunnel_z)^2),
    plate_diff = sqrt((plate_x - prev_plate_x)^2 + (plate_z - prev_plate_z)^2),
    velo_diff = release_speed-prev_pitch_velo,
    movement_diff=sqrt((pfx_x-prev_pfx_x)^2+(pfx_z-prev_pfx_z)^2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  drop_na(release_diff, early_diff, tunnel_diff, plate_diff, velo_diff, movement_diff)%>%
  filter(pitch_type!=prev_pitch_type)

#Calculates PCA scores for 2026 data
pca_scores_2026 <- predict(pca_model, newdata = paired_pitches_2026)

#Adds rows to dataset
paired_pitches_2026$PC1 <- pca_scores_2026[, "PC1"]
paired_pitches_2026$PC2 <- pca_scores_2026[, "PC2"]
paired_pitches_2026<- paired_pitches_2026%>%
  mutate(
    # Z-score against the 2024/2025 baseline
    PC1_z = (PC1 - PC1mean) / PC1sd,
    PC2_z = (PC2 - PC2mean) / PC2sd,
    Combined_Score = PC1_z + PC2_z,
    Standardized_Score=(Combined_Score - combinedmean)*-1,
    #Tunnel+ against 2024/2025 Baseline
    Tunnel_Plus = 100 + ((Standardized_Score/ combinedsd) * 10)
  )
#Leaderboard for best tunneling pitches
pitch_pair_leaderboard_2026<-paired_pitches_2026 %>%
  mutate(
    pitch_sequence = paste(prev_pitch_type, pitch_type, sep = " + ")
  ) %>%
  group_by(player_name, pitch_sequence) %>%
  filter(n() >= 5) %>% 
  summarize(
    total_thrown = n(),
    average_tunnel_value = mean(Combined_Score),
    tunnel_90 = quantile(Combined_Score, probs = 0.90, na.rm = TRUE),
    average_woba= mean(estimated_woba_using_speedangle, na.rm=TRUE),
    whiff_percentage=mean(is_whiff),
    called_strike_percentage=mean(is_called_strike),
    run_value = mean(delta_pitcher_run_exp),
    movement_diff = mean(movement_diff),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Tunnel_Plus = 100 - (((average_tunnel_value - pairmean) / pairsd) * 10)
  )%>%
  arrange(desc(Tunnel_Plus))
```

```{r}
#Regression models for 2026 data
tunnel_model_2026 <- lm(delta_pitcher_run_exp ~ Standardized_Score, data = paired_pitches_2026)
contact_model_2026<-lm(estimated_woba_using_speedangle~Standardized_Score, data = paired_pitches_2026)
whiff_model_2026<-glm(is_whiff~Standardized_Score, data=paired_pitches_2026, family=binomial)
called_strike_model_2026<-glm(is_called_strike~Standardized_Score, data=paired_pitches_2026, family=binomial)
```

```{r}
jack_tunnel_data<-read.csv("jack_tunnel.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA", "-"))
```

```{r}
#The release point metrics were all over the map because of rapsodo being calibrated differently each session
release_point<-jack_tunnel_data%>%
  mutate(
    real_date=substr(Date, 1, 15)
  )%>%
  group_by(real_date)%>%
  summarize(
    total_thrown = n(),
    average_release_height = mean(Release.Height, na.rm=TRUE),

```

```{r}
jack_tunnel_data<-jack_tunnel_data%>%
  mutate(
    real_date=substr(Date, 1, 15),
    Pitch.Type=ifelse(Pitch.Type=="Cutter", "Slider", Pitch.Type),
  )%>%
  group_by(real_date) %>%
  #Normalizing release side via linear shift
  mutate(
    session_mean = mean(Release.Side, na.rm = TRUE),
    adjustment_offset = -2.6 - session_mean,
    Release.Side = Release.Side + adjustment_offset
    
  ) %>%
  select(-session_mean, -adjustment_offset) %>%
  ungroup()
```

```{r}
clean_jack_tunnel_data<-jack_tunnel_data%>%
  #Calculate pitch trajectory using kinematics
  mutate(
    Velocity_fps=Velocity*(22/15),
    Horizontal.Angle = Horizontal.Angle * (pi / 180),
    Release.Angle = Release.Angle * (pi / 180),
    x0=Release.Side,
    z0=Release.Height,
    vx0=Velocity_fps*sin(Horizontal.Angle),
    vy0=-Velocity_fps*cos(Horizontal.Angle)*cos(Release.Angle),
    vz0=Velocity_fps*sin(Release.Angle),
    #Acceleration due to drag of basebal source: Sports Math Textbook
    ay=0.0018*vy0^2,
    tf=quad(ay,vy0,55),
    ax=(2*HB..trajectory./12)/(tf^2),
    az=(2*VB..trajectory./12)/(tf^2),
    t40= quad(ay,vy0,40),
    x40 = x0 + (vx0 * t40) + (0.5 * ax * (t40^2)),
    z40 = z0 + (vz0 * t40) + (0.5 * az * (t40^2)),
    t_tunnel= quad(ay,vy0, 28.3),
    tunnel_x = x0 + (vx0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * ax * (t_tunnel^2)),
    tunnel_z = z0 + (vz0 * t_tunnel) + (0.5 * (az-32.174) * (t_tunnel^2)),
    plate_x = x0 + (vx0 * tf) + (0.5 * ax * (tf^2)),
    plate_z = z0 + (vz0 * tf) + (0.5 * (az - 32.174) * (tf^2))
  )
```

```{r}
jack_paired_pitches<-clean_jack_tunnel_data%>%
  #Pair each pitch with its previous
  mutate(
    prev_pitch_type=lag(Pitch.Type),
    prev_pitch_velo=lag(Velocity),
    prev_x0=lag(Release.Side),
    prev_z0=lag(Release.Height),
    prev_x40 = lag(x40),
    prev_z40 = lag (z40),
    prev_tunnel_x = lag(tunnel_x),
    prev_tunnel_z = lag(tunnel_z),
    prev_plate_x = lag(plate_x),
    prev_plate_z = lag(plate_z),
    release_diff = sqrt((x0 - prev_x0)^2 + (z0 - prev_z0)^2),
    early_diff = sqrt((x40 - prev_x40)^2 + (z40 - prev_z40)^2),
    tunnel_diff = sqrt((tunnel_x - prev_tunnel_x)^2 + (tunnel_z - prev_tunnel_z)^2),
    plate_diff = sqrt((plate_x - prev_plate_x)^2 + (plate_z - prev_plate_z)^2),
  )%>%
  select(
    Pitch.Type,
    prev_pitch_type,
    Velocity,
    prev_pitch_velo,
    x0,
    prev_x0,
    z0,
    prev_z0,
    release_diff,
    early_diff,
    tunnel_diff,
    plate_diff
  )%>%
  na.omit%>%
  filter(Pitch.Type!=prev_pitch_type)%>%
  #Removes extreme outliers
  filter(release_diff<=3)
```

```{r}

  mutate(

    PC1_z = (PC1 - PC1mean) / PC1sd,
    PC2_z = (PC2 - PC2mean) / PC2sd,
    Combined_Score = (PC1_z + PC2_z)*-1,
    Tunnel_Plus = round(100+(((Combined_Score - combinedmean) / combinedsd) * 10))
  )
#Calculate Tunnel+ for using baselines form 2024/2025 data
jack_pitch_pair_leaderboard<-jack_paired_pitches %>%
  mutate(
    pitch_sequence = paste(prev_pitch_type, Pitch.Type, sep = " + ")
  ) %>%
  group_by(pitch_sequence) %>%
  summarize(
    total_thrown = n(),
    average_tunnel_value = median(Combined_Score, na.rm=TRUE),
    tunnel_90=quantile(Combined_Score, 0.9, na.rm=TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )%>%
  mutate(
    Tunnel_Plus = round(100+(((average_tunnel_value - pairmean) / pairsd) * 10))
  )
```

## My Own Tunneling:

As a college pitcher, I thought it would be interesting to evaluate how
well my pitches tunnel together. My school has a Rapsodo which we use to
collect data during bullpen sessions, so I was able to use that data to
calculate the metrics needed to find my own Tunnel+ values. I used
release point, velocity, and horizontal and vertical break data to
determine the trajectory of the pitch and calculate positions at 40
feet, the tunnel point, and the plate.

One of the biggest challenges with this approach was the quality of the
tracking data. Rapsodo is much less precise than the Hawkeye system used
in Major League Baseball, particularly when measuring release points.
Before each bullpen, the only calibration we perform is setting the unit
at the correct distance from home plate. We do our best to center the
Rapsodo on the plate and align it parallel to home plate, but small
setup errors are unavoidable. While these inaccuracies have little
effect on the velocity and pitch movement data that we typically
analyze, they can significantly impact the horizontal release point
("release side"). As a result, each bullpen session in my dataset had a
noticeably different average release side depending on how accurately
the Rapsodo was aligned. 

I attempted to combat this through normalizing each session by applying
a linear shift to each session, standardizing my mean release side to
2.6 feet (first-base side), which aligns with my true delivery. However,
even after applying the linear shift many of the sessions still had
outlier release points that didn’t seem reasonable and larger spreads
than expected. This led me to conclude that portable Rapsodo tracking
simply lacks the exactness required for precise release-point modeling.
Because of this, my confidence in the exact Tunnel+ outputs for these
bullpens is relatively low.

Even with those limitations, looking at overall trends was interesting.
My best tunneling pitches seem to be my Curveball/Changeup and
Curveball/Slider. This makes sense because these pitches have similar
movement. Especially in bullpens where I’m not throwing my hardest, the
movement profiles of these three pitches tend to blend together. 

The relationship I was most interested in was which pitch tunneled best
with my fastball. It seemed to be my slider which is what I expected and
affirms how I tend to use it. One of my favorite sequences against a
right-handed batter is a fastball that starts inside and finishes over
the middle of the plate, followed by a slider that begins on nearly the
same trajectory before breaking farther inside. This has been a pretty
effective sequence for me and due to the two pitches having a similar
initial flight path before breaking apart, the slider often induces a
swing-and-miss or weak contact.

While looking at my Rapsodo data was really cool, the lower quality data
and small sample size (I only had 118 total pitch pairs, 76 of which
were fastball slider pairs) made it hard to get a clear view of my own
tunneling and how I compare to major league pitchers. In the future I’m
going to attempt to get more and better data to see if I can learn
anything more about myself as a player.

## Limitations and Future Work:

### The Constant Acceleration Assumption

The spatial checkpoints used in this model (such as the pitch location
at 40 feet and the tunnel point) were calculated using basic kinematics
derived from Statcast's standard 9-parameter tracking data. This relies
on the assumption of constant acceleration. As a result, it cannot fully
account for non-linear aerodynamic forces such drag and Seam-Shifted
Wake (SSW) that can alter a pitch's trajectory. A future, more precise
iteration of this model would utilize frame-by-frame optical tracking
data rather than derived physics equations.

### The Batter's Visual Perspective

Tunnel+ evaluates the absolute 2D distance between pitches at specific
spatial checkpoints. However, in reality, a tunnel is a matter of visual
perception rather than absolute geometry. Because a batter stands
offsetted in the batter's box, their view of the pitch plane is angled.
A two-inch horizontal separation between two pitches presents a
completely different visual overlap to a left-handed hitter than a
right-handed hitter. Future work could involve projecting these 2D
coordinates into a true visual angle based on the batter's specific eye
level and handedness, measuring the deception rather than raw distance.

### Strategic Intent

One of the downsides of evaluating every pitch sequence and aggregating
them all into a single Tunnel+ score is that the model assumes that
every pitch is meant to tunnel off of the previous one. In actual
baseball strategy, this is not the case. Pitchers frequently utilize
"contrast pitches" such as throwing a high four-seam fastball
immediately after a low curveball specifically to change a batter’s eye
level and disrupt their visual baseline. Because the metric evaluates
spatial separation, these intentionally different sequences grade out as
poor tunnels, which can artificially drag down the aggregate score of
pitchers who heavily utilize eye-level shifts in their pitch calling.
Future iterations could involve filtering out these purposefully
non-tunneling sequences before applying a universal tunneling score.

### Follow-Up Using Full 2026 Data

Data from the first week of the 2026 season was used to test whether the
impact of Tunnel+ on an individual pitch's success persists across
multiple years. A similar follow-up analysis will be conducted to
determine whether a pitcher's Tunnel+ in prior datasets can accurately
predict their 2026 Tunnel+. Because the 2026 MLB season is currently at
the All-Star break, I am waiting for the conclusion of the regular
season to run this year-over-year stability testing.
